newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Merrill Lynch downgrades Hungary market to neutral.
newsitem.headline: Merrill Lynch downgrades Hungary market to neutral.

text.p: Merrill Lynch said on Monday it downgraded its stance towards Hungarian shares due to the Budapest bourse's vulnerability to international market sentiment.
"We are downgrading our recommendation for the Hungarian market as a whole from overweight to neutral," analysts Ed Butchart and Tom Chadwick said in a report on Hungary, dated August 14.

"The high level of foreign participation in the Hungarian market makes it more vulnerable to swings in international investor sentiment, and any growth in nervousness about U.S. equities could be expected to impact on Hungarian equities."
Merrill Lynch's downgrading of the Hungarian market followed a series of downward revisions for individual stocks such as chemicals BorsodChem, pharmaceuticals Egis and oil company MOL.

Merrill Lynch, however, saw upside potential for domestic-oriented stocks such as home improvement product maker Graboplast, retailer Fotex and trading group Skala-Coop, as Hungarian consumer demand picks up.
It also continued to rate pharmaceuticals Richter as a buy.

The report said that, besides international influence on stock prices, Hungary is also less attractive because of its current market valuation as a result of which investors may begin to look elsewhere for value.
Whilst Hungary is currently trading on a P/E ratio of 21.7 on estimated 1997 earnings, for Poland the figure is 13.7 and for the Czech Republic 11.4, the analysts said.
The Budapest bourse's medium-term outlook remained positive, however, with the 1998 elections representing little risk factor.
"Medium-term prospects for the Hungarian market remain positive, with earnings boosted by continued progress at the microeconomic level and a steadily reviving economy," the analysts said.
"Parliamentary elections scheduled for 1998 may create some inevitable uncertainties, but we consider the prospects good for the re-election of the current government."
